claim: Decisions about the behavioral significance of sensory stimuli often require comparing sensory inference of what we are looking at to internal models of what we are looking for.
source: Decisions about the behavioral significance of sensory stimuli often require comparing sensory inference of what we are looking at to internal models of what we are looking for.
evidence: This is a general statement about decision-making processes that draws from established understanding in cognitive neuroscience.

claim: LIP is involved in transforming sensory information into decision-related signals through sequential processing of visual features and selection of target-stimuli.
source: First, the sequential processing of visual features and the selection of target-stimuli suggest that LIP is involved in transforming sensory information into decision-related signals.
evidence: This claim is supported by neuronal recordings showing temporal dynamics of feature processing and target selection.

claim: LIP plays a role in detecting target stimuli by comparing bottom-up sensory inputs (what the monkeys were looking at) and top-down cognitive encoding inputs (what the monkeys were looking for).
source: Second, the patterns of color and motion selectivity and their impact on decision-related encoding suggest that LIP plays a role in detecting target stimuli by comparing bottom-up sensory inputs (what the monkeys were looking at) and top-down cognitive encoding inputs (what the monkeys were looking for).
evidence: This is supported by observed patterns of selectivity and their relationship to decision-related encoding in the recorded data.

claim: Space-based attention (SBA) and feature-based attention (FBA) increase the activity of cortical visual neurons selective to the relevant features and positions in V4.
source: A large corpus of studies has shown that both space-based attention (SBA) and feature-based attention (FBA) increase the activity of cortical visual neurons selective to the relevant features and positions (e.g. from V4 [Reynolds et al., 2000; Connor et al., 1997; McAdams and Maunsell, 2000] or MT [Martinez-Trujillo and Treue, 2004; Seidemann and Newsome, 1999]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Space-based attention (SBA) and feature-based attention (FBA) increase the activity of cortical visual neurons selective to the relevant features and positions in MT.
source: A large corpus of studies has shown that both space-based attention (SBA) and feature-based attention (FBA) increase the activity of cortical visual neurons selective to the relevant features and positions (e.g. from V4 [Reynolds et al., 2000; Connor et al., 1997; McAdams and Maunsell, 2000] or MT [Martinez-Trujillo and Treue, 2004; Seidemann and Newsome, 1999]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on MT.

claim: Attention-dependent gain modulations strengthen the bottom-up flow of relevant information and facilitate their integration and representation by downstream areas.
source: Recently, we proposed that these attention-dependent gain modulations strengthen the bottom-up flow of relevant information and facilitate their integration and representation by downstream areas (Ibos and Freedman, 2014, 2016).
evidence: This is a proposal from the authors' previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Both SBA and FBA modulations of lateral intraparietal area (LIP) neurons were consistent with LIP linearly integrating inputs from attention-modulated activity in upstream visual cortical areas.
source: Specifically, we showed that both SBA and FBA modulations of lateral intraparietal area (LIP) neurons were consistent with LIP linearly integrating inputs from attention-modulated activity in upstream visual cortical areas.
evidence: This refers to findings from the authors' previous studies.

claim: LIP has been proposed to encode stimuli behavioral salience.
source: LIP has been proposed to encode stimuli behavioral salience (Ipata et al., 2009; Bisley and Goldberg, 2003, 2010; Arcizet et al., 2011; Gottlieb et al., 1998; Leathers and Olson, 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: LIP has been proposed to transform sensory evidence into decisions about the target of saccadic eye movements.
source: to transform sensory evidence into decisions about the target of saccadic eye movements (Leon and Shadlen, 1998; Shadlen and Newsome, 2001; Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Huk and Shadlen, 2005)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LIP has been proposed to encode cognitive signals such as rules or abstract categories independently of LIP's role in spatial processing.
source: or to encode cognitive signals such as rules (Stoet and Snyder, 2004) or abstract categories (Freedman and Assad, 2006; Swaminathan and Freedman, 2012; Sarma et al., 2016) independently of LIP's role in spatial processing (Rishel et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Both monkeys performed the task with high accuracy as more than 85% of trials were hits, less than 10% were misses, and less than 5% were false-alarms.
source: Both monkeys performed the task with high accuracy (Figure 2A) as more than 85% of trials were hits, less than 10% were misses, and less than 5% were false-alarms.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral performance data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Monkeys correctly ignored test stimulus A during sample B trials and test stimulus B during sample A trials.
source: Moreover, analyses of stimuli triggering the false-alarm responses (Figure 2B) revealed that monkeys correctly ignored test stimulus A during sample B trials and test stimulus B during sample A trials.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of false-alarm responses shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 201 individual LIP neurons were recorded while monkeys performed the tasks (74 during two-location and 127 during one-location DCM tasks).
source: We recorded the activity of 201 individual LIP neurons while monkeys performed the tasks (74 during two-location and 127 during one-location DCM tasks).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental data collection.

claim: Neuron #1 responded preferentially to test stimulus B independently (at least in the initial phase of the response) of its match status.
source: Selectivity to the identity of stimuli is exemplified by neuron #1 (Figure 3A, left panel). This neuron responded preferentially to test stimulus B independently (at least in the initial phase of the response) of its match status.
evidence: This is supported by the neuronal response data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Neuron #1 was identity-selective from 86 ms to 299 ms after stimulus onset.
source: This neuron was identity-selective from 86 ms to 299 ms after stimulus onset (Figure 3, black horizontal line in the ROC panel, Wilcoxon test, Bonferroni corrected, p<0.01)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the neuronal response shown in Figure 3.

claim: Neuron #1 became selective to the match status of the stimuli 209 ms after stimulus onset.
source: and became selective to the match status of the stimuli 209 ms after stimulus onset (Figure 3, grey horizontal line in the ROC panel, Wilcoxon test, Bonferroni corrected, p<0.01)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the neuronal response shown in Figure 3.

claim: Example neuron #2 illustrates selectivity to the match status of the stimuli (starting 53 ms after stimulus onset), independent of their identity.
source: Example neuron #2 (Figure 3B) illustrates selectivity to the match status of the stimuli (starting 53 ms after stimulus onset), independent of their identity (left panel).
evidence: This is supported by the neuronal response data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The absence of selectivity to target stimuli located outside neuron #2's RF suggests that such selectivity cannot be attributed to a motor-preparation signal.
source: The absence of selectivity to target stimuli located outside this neuron's RF (right panel) suggests that such selectivity cannot be attributed to a motor-preparation signal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial specificity of the neuronal response.

claim: Neuron #3 responded preferentially to test stimulus A compared to test stimulus B (starting from 86 ms after stimulus onset).
source: Neuron #3 (Figure 3C) responded preferentially to test stimulus A compared to test stimulus B (starting from 86 ms after stimulus onset)
evidence: This is supported by the neuronal response data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Neuron #3 responded preferentially to target stimuli compared to opposite-target stimuli (starting from 124 ms after stimulus onset).
source: but also to target stimuli compared to opposite-target stimuli (starting from 124 ms after stimulus onset).
evidence: This is supported by the neuronal response data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Neuron #4 responded preferentially to target compared to opposite-target stimuli (starting 103 ms and 171 ms after stimulus onset during attention IN and attention OUT respectively).
source: For example, neuron #4 (Figure 3D) responded preferentially to target compared to opposite-target stimuli (starting 103 ms and 171 ms after stimulus onset during attention IN and attention OUT respectively)
evidence: This is supported by the neuronal response data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: A large fraction of LIP neurons (N = 147/201) showed selectivity for the identity and/or the match status of the stimuli.
source: After this correction, we observed that a large fraction of LIP neurons (N = 147/201; sliding Wilcoxon test (200 ms window), Bonferroni corrected, p<0.01) showed selectivity for the identity (N = 92; 51/67 for monkey N, 41/70 for monkey M, Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and/or the match status of the stimuli (N = 103; 34/67 for monkey N, 69/80 for monkey M).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neuronal responses across the population.

claim: 92 LIP neurons showed identity selectivity (51/67 for monkey N, 41/70 for monkey M).
source: showed selectivity for the identity (N = 92; 51/67 for monkey N, 41/70 for monkey M, Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neuronal responses.

claim: 103 LIP neurons showed match status selectivity (34/67 for monkey N, 69/80 for monkey M).
source: and/or the match status of the stimuli (N = 103; 34/67 for monkey N, 69/80 for monkey M).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neuronal responses.

claim: 48/147 neurons showed significant selectivity for both identity and match status (18/67 for monkey N, 30/80 for monkey M).
source: In addition, 48/147 neurons (18/67 for monkey N, 30/80 for monkey M) showed significant selectivity for both types of information.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of neuronal responses.

claim: The population of LIP neurons selective to either the identity of test stimuli and/or their match-status (N = 147) forms a continuum from purely identity-selective neurons (VDI = 1) to mixed identity and match/non-match selectivity (VDI~ = 0) to purely match-selective neurons (VDI=−1).
source: The VDI indicates that the population of LIP neurons selective to either the identity of test stimuli and/or their match-status (N = 147) forms a continuum from purely identity-selective neurons (VDI = 1) to mixed identity and match/non-match selectivity (VDI~ = 0) to purely match-selective neurons (VDI=−1).
evidence: This is based on the visuo-decision index calculated from the neuronal data.

claim: Identity-selectivity (N = 92, mean latency = 101.0 ms ± 72 ms) rose significantly earlier than match-selectivity (N = 103, mean latency = 187.3 ms ± 67 ms; t test, p=2*10−15).
source: First, a direct comparison of each signal's latency (black vertical ticks in Figure 4A left and middle panel, see Materials and methods) revealed that identity-selectivity (N = 92, mean latency = 101.0 ms ± 72 ms) rose significantly earlier than match-selectivity (N = 103, mean latency = 187.3 ms ± 67 ms; t test, p=2*10−15; Figure 4B, left panel).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison of signal latencies shown in Figure 4.

claim: For neurons selective for both signals (N = 48), identity selectivity latency (mean latency: 107.8 ms ± 68 ms) was significantly earlier than match selectivity latency (mean latency: 191.6 ms ± 65 ms; paired t test, p=1×10−7).
source: This is not due to higher firing rates of identity-selective neurons (N = 92) compared to match-selective neurons (N = 103) since paired comparisons of latencies for neurons selective for both signals (N = 48) revealed a similar dynamic (mean latency: stimulus identity: 107.8 ms ± 68 ms; match selectivity: 191.6 ms ± 65 ms; paired t test, p=1×10−7).
evidence: This is supported by paired statistical comparison controlling for firing rate differences.

claim: Linear classifiers could decode the identity of test stimuli (0 ms after stimulus onset) prior to their match status (93 ms after stimulus onset).
source: We found that linear classifiers could decode, above the level expected by chance (50%), the identity of test stimuli (0 ms after stimulus onset) prior to their match status (93 ms after stimulus onset; Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by SVM classifier analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The serial representation of identity and target status in LIP population suggests a role in transforming sensory information into a decision about the match status of test stimuli.
source: This serial representation of identity and target status in LIP population suggests a role in transforming sensory information into a decision about the match status of test stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal dynamics of different types of selectivity.

claim: At the population level (N = 147), the magnitude of correlation between firing rate and RT (r) covaried with each neuron's VDI (correlation coefficient = 0.32, p=7×10−5).
source: At the population level (N = 147), the magnitude of this correlation (r) covaried with each neuron's VDI (Figure 5B, correlation coefficient = 0.32, p=7×10−5).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Match-selectivity, but not identity-selectivity, reflects a process which covaries with monkeys' decisions about the relevance of the stimuli.
source: The stronger the influence of match-selectivity compared to identity selectivity, the larger the negative correlation, suggesting that match-selectivity, but not identity-selectivity, reflects a process which covaries with monkeys' decisions about the relevance of the stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between VDI and choice probability.

claim: There was an over-presentation of target during the first test period compared to the three successive ones (ANOVA, p=2×10−7).
source: We observed an over-presentation of target during the first test period compared to the three successive ones (Figure 5C, ANOVA, p=2×10−7).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of target presentation timing shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Bilateral match selectivity signals could account for the match selectivity of 20/41 neurons (permutation test, p<0.05).
source: A permutation test (see Materials and methods) revealed that bilateral match selectivity signals could account for the match selectivity of 20/41 neurons (Figure 6B, permutation test, p<0.05) as they were selective independently of the spatial location of match stimuli.
evidence: This is supported by permutation test analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Removing 20 bilaterally match selective neurons from the pool of 60 neurons did not change the finding of an inverse correlation between choice probability (r-values) and VDI (p=0.01).
source: Removing these 20 bilaterally match selective neurons from the pool of 60 neurons in Figure 5A did not change the finding of an inverse correlation between choice probability (r-values, linking each neuron's dynamics and behavioral reaction times) and VDI (Figure 6C, p=0.01).
evidence: This is supported by reanalysis after removing bilateral neurons shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A population of LIP neurons showed match-selectivity that was independent of non-spatial processes (including motor-preparation), suggesting a role in decision-related computation independent of motor-related processing.
source: Nevertheless, we were able to identify a population of LIP neurons showing match-selectivity that was independent of non-spatial processes (including motor-preparation), suggesting a role in decision-related computation independent of motor-related processing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial specificity analysis of match-selective neurons.

claim: The averaged normalized firing rate (N = 147/201) to target, color-match, direction-match, and opposite-target stimuli reveals a gradient of responses: target and opposite-target stimuli triggered the largest and smallest responses, respectively, while color and direction-match stimuli triggered intermediate responses.
source: The averaged normalized firing rate (N = 147/201, Figure 7A, top left panel) to each of these stimuli reveals a gradient of responses: target and opposite-target stimuli triggered the largest and smallest responses, respectively, while color and direction-match stimuli triggered intermediate responses.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of normalized firing rates shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The additivity-index was significantly negatively correlated with each neuron's VDI (correlation coefficient = −0.26, p=0.001).
source: This additivity-index (Figure 7A, right panel) was significantly negatively correlated with each neuron's VDI (correlation coefficient = −0.26, p=0.001).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Visual (positive VDI) neurons' additivity-indices were centered on 0, reflecting additive encoding of conjunction of features.
source: Visual (positive VDI) neurons' additivity-indices were centered on 0, reflecting additive encoding of conjunction of features
evidence: This is based on analysis of the additivity index distribution for visually selective neurons.

claim: Identity-selective neurons express their selectivity by linearly pooling bottom-up color and direction encoding.
source: suggesting that identity-selective neurons express their selectivity by linearly pooling bottom-up color and direction encoding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the additivity analysis for identity-selective neurons.

claim: Decision-related neurons (negative VDI) showed apparent super-additive (positive additivity-index) encoding of conjunction of features.
source: On the contrary, decision-related neurons (negative VDI) showed apparent super-additive (positive additivity-index) encoding of conjunction of features.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the additivity index for decision-related neurons.

claim: FBA shifts LIP's representation of individual features toward the relevant direction and color in a manner consistent with bottom-up integration of sensory information.
source: We previously showed that FBA shifts LIP's representation of individual features toward the relevant direction and color (Ibos and Freedman, 2014, 2016) in a manner consistent with bottom-up integration of sensory information.
evidence: This refers to findings from the authors' previous studies.

claim: The amplitude of feature-tuning shifts depended on the strength of each LIP neuron's feature-selectivity.
source: Moreover, we showed that the amplitude of these feature-tuning shifts depended on the strength of each LIP neuron's feature-selectivity, which presumably reflects the connectivity between individual LIP neurons and upstream cortical visual neurons.
evidence: This refers to findings from the authors' previous studies.

claim: There was a significant correlation between each neuron's VDI and the amplitude of color tuning shifts (correlation coefficient = 0.63, p=1×10−17).
source: As predicted, we found a significant correlation between each neuron's VDI and the amplitude of feature-tuning shifts (for color: correlation coefficient = 0.63, p=1×10−17; for direction: correlation coefficient = −0.26, p=0.001)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between VDI and feature-tuning shifts.

claim: There was a significant correlation between each neuron's VDI and the amplitude of direction tuning shifts (correlation coefficient = −0.26, p=0.001).
source: As predicted, we found a significant correlation between each neuron's VDI and the amplitude of feature-tuning shifts (for color: correlation coefficient = 0.63, p=1×10−17; for direction: correlation coefficient = −0.26, p=0.001)
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis between VDI and feature-tuning shifts.

claim: FBA had a larger impact on neurons involved in encoding decision-related signals than on visually selective neurons.
source: showing that FBA had a larger impact on neurons involved in encoding decision-related signals than on visually selective neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between VDI and feature-tuning shifts.

claim: Match-selectivity in LIP is a composite signal resulting from the pooling of bottom-up sensory information with additional extraretinal signals.
source: This relationship suggests that match-selectivity in LIP is a composite signal resulting from the pooling of bottom-up sensory information with additional extraretinal signals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between FBA effects and VDI.

claim: LIP is composed of a visuo-decision continuum of neurons involved to different degrees in (1) the integration of bottom-up sensory inputs, (2) the linear grouping of these disparate sensory signals and (3) their transformation into a signal related to monkeys' decisions about the relevance of the visual stimuli.
source: We propose that LIP is composed of a visuo-decision continuum of neurons involved to different degrees in (1) the integration of bottom-up sensory inputs, (2) the linear grouping of these disparate sensory signals and (3) their transformation into a signal related to monkeys' decisions about the relevance of the visual stimuli.
evidence: This is a synthesis and interpretation of all the findings presented in the study.

claim: The stereotypical ramping activity preceding the execution of saccadic eye movement is likely to be driven to a large degree by processes related to preparing the upcoming saccade rather than by the motion stimulus or by the accumulation of sensory evidence.
source: As noted by several studies (Filimon et al., 2013; Freedman and Assad, 2016), the stereotypical ramping activity preceding the execution of saccadic eye movement (Leon and Shadlen, 1998; Shadlen and Newsome, 2001; Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Huk and Shadlen, 2005) is likely to be driven to a large degree by processes related to preparing the upcoming saccade—which have been extensively shown to modulate the activity of LIP neurons (Gnadt and Andersen, 1988; Barash et al., 1991)—rather than by the motion stimulus or by the accumulation of sensory evidence.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: The pre-saccadic activity of LIP neurons has long been associated with the intention of performing a saccadic eye movement toward the RF.
source: This is especially evident since the pre-saccadic activity of LIP neurons has long been associated with the intention of performing a saccadic eye movement toward the RF (Gnadt and Andersen, 1988; Andersen and Buneo, 2002; Bracewell et al., 1996; Mazzoni et al., 1996)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reversible inactivation of LIP does not alter monkeys' ability to perform sensorimotor transformation.
source: that reversible inactivation of LIP does not alter monkeys' ability to perform such sensorimotor transformation (Katz et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: LIP multiplexes and independently encodes cognitive (abstract category-selectivity) and saccade-related signals.
source: Our approach is supported by studies showing that LIP multiplexes and independently encodes cognitive (abstract category-selectivity) and saccade-related signals (Rishel et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A large fraction of LIP neurons encoded the relevance of stimuli independently of monkeys' behavioral responses.
source: Although our task was not designed to specifically distinguish between detection, decision-making and motor-preparation, a large fraction of LIP neurons encoded the relevance of stimuli independently of monkeys' behavioral responses.
evidence: This is based on the analysis of unilateral vs bilateral match selectivity.

claim: Representation of individual features in LIP is consistent with the linear bottom-up integration of the activity of populations of feature-selective neurons in upstream visual areas.
source: Recently, we showed that representation of individual features in LIP is consistent with the linear bottom-up integration of the activity of populations of feature-selective neurons in upstream visual areas (Ibos and Freedman, 2014, 2016).
evidence: This refers to findings from the authors' previous studies.

claim: According to Bayesian inference theory, decision-variables are computed by comparing statistical inferences about the stimuli subjects are looking at to an internal model of the stimuli subjects are looking for.
source: According to Bayesian inference theory (Kersten et al., 2004), decision-variables (match-selectivity in our data) are computed by comparing statistical inferences (Parker and Newsome, 1998) (identity-selectivity in our data) about the stimuli subjects are looking at to an internal model of the stimuli subjects are looking for.
evidence: This claim draws on established theoretical frameworks cited in the text.

claim: The super-additivity observed for match-selective neurons in LIP hypothetically is the outcome of a computation related to the comparison of the identity of the stimuli with top-down signals, presumably originating in PFC, related to internal models of which features are behaviorally relevant.
source: The super-additivity observed for match-selective neurons in LIP hypothetically is the outcome of a computation related to the comparison of the identity of the stimuli with top-down signals, presumably originating in PFC (Mante et al., 2013), related to internal models of which features are behaviorally relevant.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the super-additivity finding, with reference to PFC involvement.

claim: The selectivity for sample identity across each trial epoch could reflect the integration of top-down signals related to the identity of the relevant stimuli kept in working memory.
source: The selectivity for sample identity across each trial epoch (Figure 7C) could reflect the integration of top-down signals related to the identity of the relevant stimuli kept in working memory.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the sample identity encoding shown in Figure 7C.

claim: LIP encodes all the information required to solve the DCM task: (1) the information being encoded in working memory; (2) the stimuli monkeys were looking for; (3) the stimuli monkeys were currently looking at; (4) the monkeys' match/non-match decisions; (5) the monkeys' behavioral responses.
source: Finally, we showed that LIP encodes all the information required to solve the DCM task: (1) the information being encoded in working memory; (2) the stimuli monkeys were looking for; (3) the stimuli monkeys were currently looking at; (4) the monkeys' match/non-match decisions; (5) the monkeys' behavioral responses.
evidence: This is a summary of the various types of information encoded by LIP neurons as demonstrated throughout the study.

claim: Stimuli were 6° diameter circular patches of 476 random colored dots moving at a speed of 10°/s with 100% coherence.
source: Stimuli were 6° diameter circular patches of 476 random colored dots moving at a speed of 10°/s with 100% coherence.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental stimuli.

claim: All stimuli were generated using the LAB color space (1976 CIE L*a*b), and all colors were measured as isoluminant in experimental condition using a luminance meter.
source: All stimuli were generated using the LAB color space (1976 CIE L*a*b), and all colors were measured as isoluminant in experimental condition using a luminance meter (Minolta).
evidence: This is a direct description of the stimulus generation and calibration methods.

claim: Gaze position was measured with an optical eye tracker at 1.0 kHz sample rate.
source: Gaze position was measured with an optical eye tracker (SR Research) at 1.0 kHz sample rate.
evidence: This is a direct description of the eye tracking methodology.

claim: LIP neuronal activity was strongly influenced by the identity of the sample stimulus during sample presentation, delay period, and prior/during the presentation of each test stimulus.
source: But, as shown in previous studies (Ibos and Freedman, 2014, 2016), LIP neuronal activity was strongly influenced by the identity of the sample stimulus (Figure 7C) during sample presentation but also during the delay period and prior/during the presentation of each test stimulus.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C and references to previous studies.

claim: Sample encoding during the delay and test periods is consistent with a role for LIP in encoding task-relevant information in short-term memory.
source: Sample encoding during the delay and test periods is consistent with a role for LIP in encoding task-relevant information in short-term memory.
evidence: This is an inference based on the persistence of sample-related activity.

claim: 24/74 neurons showed sample-related activity that mimicked identity selectivity prior to stimulus onset (Wilcoxon test, p<0.05).
source: This characteristic of the neuronal response in LIP interfered with our analysis of the dynamics of sensory selectivity as it was responsible for larger response during either sample A or sample B trials, mimicking the effect of identity selectivity on the ROC analysis prior stimulus onset in several neurons (N = 24/74, Wilcoxon test, p<0.05).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of pre-stimulus activity.
